objectives: Design an AST with discriminated-union node types.
Apply the visitor pattern for tree traversal.
Track source positions for accurate diagnostics.

slides.title: AST vs CST: shape the tree you'll actually use
slides.body:
The parser can build two related trees:

- **CST (Concrete Syntax Tree, aka parse tree)**: lossless 1:1 with the source. Every parenthesis, every comma, every whitespace span. Used by formatters (prettier, rustfmt) + refactoring tools that need to preserve trivia.
- **AST (Abstract Syntax Tree)**: drops syntactic noise. `(1 + 2)` and `1 + 2` produce the SAME AST node `BinOp(+, 1, 2)`. Easier to traverse, smaller, the right shape for semantic analysis.

Most compilers build an AST directly (skipping the explicit CST). Tools like Roslyn (.NET), rust-analyzer, swift-syntax build CSTs because they need to preserve formatting.

AST design pattern in Rust/Swift/OCaml/Haskell/TS: discriminated union per category:
```
type Expr =
  | Num(value: number)
  | Ident(name: string)
  | BinOp(op: string, left: Expr, right: Expr)
  | Call(callee: Expr, args: Expr[])
  | If(cond: Expr, then: Expr, else: Expr)
  | ...
```
In languages without sum types, use a base class + subclasses. The TS/JS world uses tagged unions: `{ type: 'BinOp', op: '+', left, right }`.

slides.title: Visitor pattern: separating traversal from operation
Source positions = good diagnostics
slides.body:
Every AST node should carry a **span**: `{ start: Position, end: Position }` where `Position = { line, column, offset }`. This lets the compiler emit:
```
error: cannot find name `flux`
   --> src/main.rs:42:13
    |
42  |     let y = flux + 1;
    |             ^^^^ help: did you mean `flex`?
```
rather than 'syntax error on line 42'.

Design decisions:
- **Position stored on every node** (clang, rust-analyzer): more memory but every diagnostic is precise.
- **Position stored only at key nodes** (compact ASTs): each node carries an offset, end-computed lazily.
- **Interned source strings**: identifiers like `x` and `y` recur thousands of times — intern to single index. rustc's `Symbol` is a `u32` index into a string table.

Modern compilers prioritize diagnostic quality. clang's error messages set the bar in 2010; rustc pushed it further with fix-it suggestions, related-info spans, multi-line error annotations. The infrastructure cost is real but pays for itself in user experience.

IDE tools (rust-analyzer, gopls, Language Server Protocol) need character-precise positions to highlight, jump-to-definition, etc. — accurate spans aren't optional for modern dev tooling.

question.question: Derive a tree-walking interpreter
question.goal: Define `eval(e: Expr, env: Map<string,number>): number` for our toy AST.
question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Tree-walking interpreter: one case per node type, recurse on subtrees}}$$ The simplest possible execution strategy. Slow (~100× slower than native code on tight loops, lots of pointer chasing) but easy to extend + debug. Real interpreters: TypeScript's `tsc` (well, just for evaluation of const expressions), MRI Ruby pre-2007, the AST tier of every JIT before tier-up.

question.question: Why do `prettier` and `rustfmt` build a CST (concrete syntax tree) instead of just an AST?
options: CSTs preserve whitespace, comments, and parenthesization — formatters need to reproduce these.
Parsing to an AST is impossible for these languages.
question.explanation: Formatters must round-trip the source — preserve comments, decide where to wrap, respect blank lines. The AST drops all of this. Formatters either build a CST OR attach trivia (comments + whitespace) to AST nodes. rustfmt's approach is the latter. prettier builds a CST-like structure with comment attachment.

hints: What does a formatter need to preserve?
slides.workedSolution: ASTs drop syntactic 'noise' (parens, whitespace, comments). Formatters need EVERY one of these to round-trip the source correctly + idiomatically. Either keep a CST (rust-analyzer style) or attach trivia to AST nodes (rustfmt style). prettier's printing algorithm needs comment + whitespace info to decide line breaks.

question.question: An expression `((((a)))) + ((((b))))` produces an AST with how many nodes (after dropping parens)?
Designing rust-quality diagnostics
question.prompt: Your team adds a beautiful-error-messages feature. What AST/CST design decisions enable diagnostics like 'expected `;`, found `}`' with the relevant spans highlighted?
Explain in two or three sentences why every AST node carries a source-position span.
question.rubric: Mentions that good diagnostics (error messages pointing at exact source location), IDE features (jump-to-definition, hover-info, completion), and tooling (linters, refactors) all require character-precise position info per node. The memory overhead is small + the user-experience win is large.
